## Russia-Arab summit invitation (May 2025)

In May 2025 Putin invited the heads of state and government of [[arab-league|Arab League]] member countries to attend the first Russia-Arab summit, scheduled for October 15 in Moscow, with the Kremlin publishing the invitation on its official website on a Saturday as Arab leaders gathered in Baghdad to discuss the war in Gaza.[{n}] Putin said Russia intended "to further actively develop constructive dialogue with the League of Arab States, as well as friendly relations with all its members," and extended the invitation to the League's Secretary-General as well.[{n}] He framed the planned meeting as taking place "in a difficult international situation," citing the "sharp escalation of the Palestinian-Israeli confrontation" and "numerous civilian casualties," and described the Arab League as "an effective mechanism for multilateral dialogue and joint response" to challenges facing the Middle East and North Africa.[{n}] Badlands commentator GhostofBasedPatrickHenry read the timing as a deliberate response to the Gulf diplomacy of the preceding week, speculating that Putin might use the Arab League as a vehicle to restore Bashar al-Assad and displace the new Damascus leadership once Western sanctions had been lifted.[{n}]

## Trump call on Ukraine (May 2025)

On May 17, 2025, [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] announced on [[truth-social|Truth Social]] that he would speak by telephone with Putin on Monday at 10:00 a.m., with the stated subjects being "stopping the 'bloodbath' that is killing, on average, more than 5,000 Russian and Ukrainian soldiers a week, and trade."[{n}] Trump said he would afterward speak separately with [[volodymyr-zelensky|Volodymyr Zelensky]] and with members of [[nato|NATO]].[{n}] Overnight into that Sunday, Ukrainian officials reported that Russia had launched its most intense drone attack against Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.[{n}] Badlands writers noted that a telephone call, unlike a summit, would generate no optics and therefore no memorable imagery, and expressed a preference for an eventual face-to-face meeting.[{n}]

## Russia-Arab summit invitation (2025)

In May 2025 Russian President [[vladimir-putin|Vladimir Putin]] invited the heads of state and government of Arab League member countries, together with the League's Secretary-General, to the first Russia-Arab summit, planned for October 15 in Moscow.[{n}] The Kremlin published the invitation on its official website while Arab leaders were gathered in Baghdad to discuss the war in Gaza.[{n}] Putin praised the organization as "an effective mechanism for multilateral dialogue and joint response to the challenges and threats faced by the peoples of the Middle East and North Africa."[{n}] At the 34th Arab League Summit held that same Saturday, regional leaders collectively condemned Israel's military actions in Gaza, called for an immediate ceasefire, and pledged financial support for the enclave's reconstruction.[{n}] Badlands commentary linked the invitation to the League's 2023 readmission of Syria after an eleven-year absence and speculated about the organization being used as a lever in a future Syrian settlement.[{n}]
entities/joe-biden:
## Hur audio recordings and cancer diagnosis (May 2025)

In May 2025 the [[wall-street-journal|Wall Street Journal]] obtained and published audio of Biden's October 2023 interviews with special counsel [[robert-hur|Robert Hur]], in which the former president can be heard at times speaking with a frail voice and struggling for the right words and dates.[{n}] The interviews spanned some five hours over two days; the Biden administration had released transcripts in March 2024 but declined to make the audio public.[{n}] Hur conducted the interviews as part of his investigation into whether Biden improperly retained classified information after leaving office as vice president at the end of Barack Obama's administration.[{n}] The recordings show Biden at times joking and in command of details and at other times pursuing long digressions and forgetting basic facts; asked where he kept his papers in 2017 and 2018, he offered a tortured timeline that mixed up his vice presidency with his Senate tenure and struggled to remember the year his son Beau died.[{n}] The release coincided with a broader Democratic reckoning over the extent of Biden's diminished faculties in office, including forthcoming books by CNN host [[jake-tapper|Jake Tapper]] and Axios reporter Alex Thompson.[{n}]

Days later it was reported that Biden had been diagnosed with an aggressive prostate cancer characterized by a Gleason score of 9 and Grade Group 5 with bone metastasis, a presentation with a five-year survival rate of roughly 30% to 40%.[{n}] Fox News senior medical analyst Marc Siegel described the disease as "the most aggressive type" with "the highest risk of spread," and noted that Biden's urinary symptoms were a further sign of advanced disease.[{n}] Badlands writers declined to celebrate the diagnosis but rejected the premise that it was newly discovered, noting that Biden himself had said he had cancer in 2022 — a remark the press waved away as a gaffe — and argued that the announcement functioned to shut down scrutiny of his mental acuity and the [[autopen-scandal|autopen]] question.[{n}] Chris Paul characterized Biden as a scapegoat whose "character" would be written out of the story at an opportune moment, a role he said he had predicted since late 2020.[{n}]

## Release of the interview audio (May 2025)

In May 2025 the [[wall-street-journal|Wall Street Journal]] obtained audio recordings of Hur's October 2023 interviews with [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]], which the Biden administration had withheld after releasing transcripts in March 2024.[{n}] The interviews ran some five hours across two days and were conducted as part of Hur's investigation into whether Biden improperly retained classified information after leaving office as vice president.[{n}] In the audio Biden at times speaks with a frail voice, struggles for words and dates, and mixes up his Senate years with his vice presidency, while at other points joking and appearing in command of details.[{n}] The recordings intensified a public reckoning among Democrats over Biden's condition in office and were cited by [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] and by Representative [[james-comer|James Comer]] as evidence bearing on the [[autopen-scandal|autopen]] question.[{n}]

## Audio release (May 2025)

The [[wall-street-journal|Wall Street Journal]] obtained and published the underlying audio of the October 2023 [[robert-hur|Hur]] interviews in May 2025, more than a year after the Biden administration released transcripts in March 2024 but refused to make the recordings public.[{n}] The tapes captured [[joe-biden|Biden]] speaking at times with a frail voice, digressing at length, mixing up his Senate tenure with his vice presidency when asked where he kept his papers in 2017 and 2018, and struggling to recall the year his son Beau died.[{n}] Their release coincided with new books on Biden's decline by [[jake-tapper|Jake Tapper]] and Alex Thompson and fed directly into Republican arguments about the [[autopen-scandal|autopen]].[{n}]

## Trump and Comer after the Hur audio (May 2025)

The May 2025 release of the [[robert-hur|Hur]] interview audio gave the autopen question fresh momentum.[{n}] [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] posted on [[truth-social|Truth Social]] that "Whoever had control of the 'AUTOPEN' is looking to be a bigger and bigger scandal by the moment."[{n}] Kentucky Republican Representative [[james-comer|James Comer]] told Fox News that the interview, conducted "many, many months prior to the heavy use of the autopen," showed that "Joe Biden wasn't capable of making decisions. He wasn't coherent."[{n}] Conservatives on social media pressed the question of who was controlling the device and whether someone else was effectively acting as president, claims The Independent noted were advanced without supporting evidence.[{n}] Badlands commentary went further, arguing that Biden's simultaneous cancer diagnosis meant "the criminals using the cancer-riddled dementia patient and his autopen are even more criminal than previously thought," and calling for [[jill-biden|Jill Biden]], the White House medical staff, the chief of staff, the cabinet, [[karine-jean-pierre|Karine Jean-Pierre]] and [[jake-sullivan|Jake Sullivan]] to answer questions under oath.[{n}]

## Autopen, Clinton posts and the Putin call (May 2025)

On Saturday, May 17, 2025, Trump used [[truth-social|Truth Social]] to attack [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]] after leaked audio of Biden's interview with special counsel [[robert-hur|Robert Hur]] became public, writing that "Whoever had control of the 'AUTOPEN' is looking to be a bigger and bigger scandal by the moment," and adding that "the biggest crime of all is that THE 2020 PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION WAS RIGGED!"[{n}] The same weekend he reshared a 2016 video captioned "THE VIDEO HILLARY CLINTON DOES NOT WANT YOU TO SEE," reviving the long-standing claim that [[bill-clinton|Bill Clinton]] and [[hillary-clinton|Hillary Clinton]] are connected to a series of deaths; the Washington Post characterized the posts as false conspiracy theories and noted Democratic warnings that such rhetoric could lead to violence.[{n}] Badlands writer Burning Bright instead read the post as a deliberate signal, noting that a sitting president had amplified "the most direct Clinton Body Count proof he could, including [[jfk-jr|JFK Jr.]]"[{n}]

Trump also announced he would speak by telephone with [[vladimir-putin|Vladimir Putin]] on Monday at 10:00 a.m. about "stopping the 'bloodbath'" in Ukraine and about trade, followed by separate calls with [[volodymyr-zelensky|Volodymyr Zelensky]] and members of [[nato|NATO]].[{n}] His administration's executive order on [[birthright-citizenship|birthright citizenship]] was simultaneously before the [[supreme-court-of-the-united-states|Supreme Court]] in the case over [[nationwide-injunctions|universal injunctions]], where Justice [[elena-kagan|Elena Kagan]] told Solicitor General [[d-john-sauer|John Sauer]] that "every court is ruling against you."[{n}]

## Trump's May 2025 "body count" posts

In May 2025 [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] reshared a 2016 video captioned "THE VIDEO HILLARY CLINTON DOES NOT WANT YOU TO SEE," which rehearsed long-standing claims tying Clinton and her husband [[bill-clinton|Bill Clinton]] to a series of deaths of people who could be seen as political opponents.[{n}] The Washington Post described the material as false conspiracy theory and situated it within what it called thousands of false or misleading statements Trump has made about political opponents across his two terms.[{n}] Badlands commentary treated the amplification of the "Clinton body count" material by a sitting president as significant in itself.[{n}] Separately, Badlands writers asserted that Syria's readmission to the [[arab-league|Arab League]] traced back to arrangements Clinton made as Secretary of State in 2012.[{n}]

## Birthright citizenship argument (May 2025)

In May 2025 Kagan questioned Solicitor General [[d-john-sauer|John Sauer]] on the practicalities of ending [[nationwide-injunctions|universal injunctions]], the central issue in a closely watched case arising from the Trump administration's executive order on [[birthright-citizenship|birthright citizenship]].[{n}] She pressed Sauer on how the [[supreme-court-of-the-united-states|Supreme Court]] would manage the flow of lower-court challenges if universal injunctions ended, and observed that the administration had been "losing uniformly" in lower courts on the substantive question.[{n}] "If I were in your shoes, there's no way I'd approach the court with this case!" she quipped, adding, "This is not a hypothetical — this is happening out there. Every court is ruling against you."[{n}] The justices had agreed in April to hear the case, which arose from three lower courts that issued national injunctions blocking [[donald-trump|Trump]]'s executive order.[{n}] Badlands commentators criticized her reference to "all the law this court has ever made" as an admission that the Court legislates, and contrasted her posture with a 2022 statement, made while [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]] was president, that "it CAN'T be right that one District Judge can stop a nationwide policy in its tracks!"[{n}]

## Birthright citizenship oral argument (May 2025)

As Solicitor General, Sauer argued the Trump administration's case before the [[supreme-court-of-the-united-states|Supreme Court]] in May 2025 on the power of lower courts to issue [[nationwide-injunctions|universal injunctions]], a dispute arising from three national injunctions blocking [[donald-trump|Trump]]'s executive order on [[birthright-citizenship|birthright citizenship]].[{n}] Justice [[elena-kagan|Elena Kagan]] pressed him on how the high court would manage lower-court challenges without universal injunctions and told him the administration had been "losing uniformly" on the substantive question, remarking, "If I were in your shoes, there's no way I'd approach the court with this case!"[{n}]

## May 2025 Supreme Court argument

The [[supreme-court-of-the-united-states|Supreme Court]] heard argument in May 2025 on whether district courts may issue universal injunctions, in a case arising from three lower courts that had blocked [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s executive order on [[birthright-citizenship|birthright citizenship]] nationwide earlier that year.[{n}] Justice [[elena-kagan|Elena Kagan]] grilled Solicitor General [[d-john-sauer|John Sauer]] on how the high court would manage the resulting flow of lower-court litigation if universal injunctions were abolished, and noted the administration had been "losing uniformly" below.[{n}] Badlands commentators pointed out that Kagan had taken the opposite position in 2022 under [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]], when she said "it CAN'T be right that one District Judge can stop a nationwide policy in its tracks," and argued that justices who shift on constitutional authority according to political calculus "effectively declare themselves illegitimate."[{n}]
concepts/birthright-citizenship:
## Universal injunctions case (May 2025)

In April 2025 the [[supreme-court-of-the-united-states|Supreme Court]] agreed to hear a case centered on birthright citizenship and the power of lower courts to rule against the executive branch, after three lower courts issued [[nationwide-injunctions|national injunctions]] blocking [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s executive order on the subject.[{n}] At argument in May, Justice [[elena-kagan|Elena Kagan]] told Solicitor General [[d-john-sauer|John Sauer]] that the administration had been "losing uniformly" in lower courts on the substantive question and that "every court is ruling against you."[{n}] Badlands commentary objected that Kagan treated four judicial decisions defining birthright citizenship as though they were law, arguing that "the Court has made zero laws."[{n}]

## Birthright citizenship and universal injunctions (2025)

The Court agreed in April 2025 to hear a case centered on [[birthright-citizenship|birthright citizenship]] and the power of lower courts to rule against the executive branch, arising from three lower courts that had issued national injunctions blocking [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s executive order.[{n}] At oral argument in May, Justice [[elena-kagan|Elena Kagan]] pressed Solicitor General [[d-john-sauer|John Sauer]] on the practicalities of ending [[nationwide-injunctions|universal injunctions]] and on how the high court would then manage the flow of lower-court challenges.[{n}] Badlands commentary used the exchange to argue that the Court's own precedents on birthright citizenship were being treated as statute, a position it rejected as constitutionally unacceptable.[{n}]
concepts/2020-election-fraud-claims:
## Trump's May 2025 restatement

Amid the release of the [[robert-hur|Hur]] audio in May 2025, [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] declared on [[truth-social|Truth Social]] that "the biggest crime of all is that THE 2020 PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION WAS RIGGED!"[{n}] Badlands writers treated the statement as vindication of their own long-running position and argued that celebrating the 2024 result while conceding the legitimacy of the 2020 count would "retroactively codif[y] the System's win in 2020."[{n}] Burning Bright argued that ceding the 2020 election to [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]] had itself been part of a plan that accelerated public awakening while affording space for operations that would have been impossible with Trump publicly in power, while maintaining that the election was nonetheless fraudulent.[{n}]

## Victory in the 2025 rerun

Dan, the pro-EU mayor of Bucharest, defeated Eurosceptic candidate [[george-simion|George Simion]] in Romania's presidential election rerun, taking 54% of the vote to Simion's 46% with more than 99% of ballots counted.[{n}] He thanked supporters for an "unprecedented mobilization" and wrote on X: "Starting tomorrow, we begin the reconstruction of Romania – a united and honest Romania, founded on respect for the law and for all its people."[{n}] Badlands commentary greeted the outcome with open skepticism, noting that the same authorities had annulled the previous election, cancelled its follow-up, and prosecuted the populist who had won it before a second populist candidate likewise fell short.[{n}]
entities/george-simion:
## Defeat in the 2025 rerun

Simion, the Eurosceptic candidate, lost Romania's presidential election rerun to pro-EU Bucharest mayor [[nicusor-dan|Nicusor Dan]], receiving 46% of the vote to Dan's 54% with more than 99% of ballots counted.[{n}] Badlands commentary framed his defeat as suspicious given that he had emerged as the successor to an earlier populist candidate whose victory was annulled and who was subsequently arrested, and who had appeared to draw that entire base of support.[{n}]
concepts/2025-romanian-presidential-elec:
## The May 2025 rerun result

The rerun that followed the annulment and the exclusion of the original populist winner was won by pro-EU Bucharest mayor [[nicusor-dan|Nicusor Dan]], who defeated Eurosceptic [[george-simion|George Simion]] 54% to 46% with more than 99% of ballots counted.[{n}] Dan credited an "unprecedented mobilization" and pledged "the reconstruction of Romania – a united and honest Romania, founded on respect for the law."[{n}] Badlands writers pointed to the sequence — nullified results, a cancelled follow-up vote, the arrest of the populist winner, and then the defeat of his successor — as grounds for doubting the official tally.[{n}]
concepts/bitcoin:
## May 2025 rally and the stablecoin bill

Bitcoin reclaimed the $100,000 level in May 2025 and surged to $106,000 on a Sunday, a level not seen since early February and close to its all-time high of almost $110,000.[{n}] Forbes reported that [[jpmorgan-chase|JPMorgan]] analysts had flipped from gold to bitcoin, predicting bitcoin would outperform gold over the remainder of 2025, even as BlackRock issued what the outlet called a stark bitcoin warning.[{n}] The rally coincided with a U.S. bill to regulate [[stablecoin|stablecoin]] issuers — formally introducing crypto into the established financial system — heading for debate in Congress that week, with some observers expecting it to pass the Senate.[{n}] Coverage tied the year's extreme price swings to [[donald-trump|Trump]]'s disruption of the global trade order and attendant predictions of dollar collapse.[{n}]

In May 2025 JPMorgan analysts flipped from gold to [[bitcoin|bitcoin]], predicting that bitcoin would outperform gold over the remainder of 2025, a call reported as the bitcoin price reclaimed $100,000 and rose to $106,000.[{n}]

## Congressional debate (May 2025)

A U.S. bill to regulate stablecoin issuers, described as formally introducing crypto into the established financial system, was scheduled for congressional debate in the week of May 19, 2025, with some observers predicting it would pass the Senate.[{n}] Its progress coincided with a [[bitcoin|bitcoin]] rally to $106,000.[{n}]

## Response to the Moody's downgrade (May 2025)

Appearing on Meet the Press after [[moodys|Moody's]] stripped the United States of its last top rating, Bessent dismissed the move: "Moody's is a lagging indicator. I think that's what everyone thinks of credit agencies."[{n}] He noted that [[larry-summers|Larry Summers]], with whom he said he does not agree on everything, had said the same of the 2011 downgrade, and drew an analogy to [[sean-duffy|Sean Duffy]]'s comments on the air traffic control system: "we didn't get here in the past 100 days."[{n}] Bessent blamed "the Biden administration and the spending that we have seen over the past four years," said the administration had inherited a 6.7% deficit-to-GDP ratio — "the highest when we weren't in a recession, not in a war" — and pledged to bring spending down and grow the economy.[{n}]

## Aftermath of the 2011 downgrade

Commentary on the May 2025 [[moodys|Moody's]] downgrade recalled that S&P's August 2011 U.S. sovereign downgrade prompted the worst single-day fall in U.S. stock prices since the global financial crisis, though the market recovered quickly.[{n}] It also noted that the Justice Department launched an investigation into S&P shortly afterward; CEO Deven Sharma left the company within a few weeks, and when the matter became a $5 billion federal lawsuit alleging that S&P had misled banks about the credibility of its ratings before the 2008 crisis, the firm called the action direct retaliation for its downgrade.[{n}]

## National Defense Area prosecutions (2025)

As Defense Secretary, Hegseth praised the establishment of the restricted National Defense Area along the U.S.-Mexico border, emphasizing its role in reducing illegal crossings and warning during a visit earlier in 2025 that "when you cross illegally, you will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law."[{n}] In May 2025 a federal judge in New Mexico, Gregory B. ## FDA restriction of the Novavax vaccine (May 2025)

Under Kennedy's leadership as Secretary of Health and Human Services, the [[food-and-drug-administration|Food and Drug Administration]] severely restricted the use of the [[novavax|Novavax]] COVID-19 vaccine, approving it only for older people and those over the age of 12 with at least one medical condition placing them at high risk from Covid.[{n}] The vaccine will not be administered to people who might seek it to protect others, meaning healthy people over 65 cannot obtain it even on behalf of an immunocompromised friend or family member.[{n}] CDC advisers had been discussing whether to recommend the vaccine only for those most at risk.[{n}]
